goals: Eliminate sensitivity to the number of client UDP flows so that all reuseport workers are used even when there are only a few flows (e.g., 7 send workers vs 6 server workers).
Avoid concentrating traffic on a small subset of workers, which previously caused per-worker saturation, long UDP queues, and dropped packets while other workers were idle.
Reduce GET p99 latency at higher offered loads (≥100k req/s) by shrinking per-worker queues and spreading rare, long SCAN requests across all workers instead of a few hotspots.
Keep the eBPF selector simple, stateless, and O(1) per packet, with no new user-space configuration or additional maps.

Preserve the server’s stateless per-request semantics and the client’s existing pipelined, reqID-based request/response handling so that responses remain correct regardless of which worker processes a given packet.
evidence: The current agent selector computes `start = reuse->hash % state->active` and then probes from that slot, which pins each client 4‑tuple to a fixed worker index, implementing per-flow consistent hashing.

With ~7 client send workers and 6 server workers, server logs show only 4–5 workers handle traffic; each active worker’s GET count per second is an integer multiple of a common base, and those multiples sum to ≈7, confirming that flows are pinned and unevenly packed into 6 buckets.

At offered rates of 50–80k req/s, these 4–5 hot workers still have headroom, so UDP and in-process queues stay short: client sent≈recv, there are no missing responses, and GET p99 latency is only a few microseconds above the synthetic 10µs delay.

At 100k and 140k req/s, total server throughput plateaus around 90–95k req/s even as offered load increases and at least one worker remains idle in each run, indicating that the bottleneck is uneven worker utilization rather than total CPU capacity.

Each worker is a single goroutine that synchronously processes GET (10µs busy-wait) and SCAN (2ms busy-wait) requests in FIFO order; although SCANs are only ~1% of requests, they dominate CPU time (~67%), so when traffic is concentrated on a few workers, those 2ms SCANs repeatedly cause head-of-line blocking for the many short GETs queued behind them.

Under high load, these hot workers’ UDP receive queues and in-process queues grow, pushing GET p99 latency from microseconds to ~0.6ms at 100k and ~5ms at 140k, and eventually overflowing so that ~222k responses are never received at 140k even though the server logs show no application-level errors.

Server-side code (handleRequest and worker setup) is fully stateless with respect to client identity: there is no state keyed by remote UDP address or 4‑tuple, only per-worker stats indexed by worker ID. This means breaking flow affinity does not threaten correctness within the current design.

On the client side, each send goroutine continuously issues requests on its UDPConn under a rate limiter without waiting for responses; a separate recv goroutine on the same UDPConn handles replies and uses embedded reqIDs for matching. Multiple outstanding requests per flow and response reordering are already supported by design, so changing worker selection per packet will not violate any ordering assumptions.
architecture: Replace the flow-sticky `reuse->hash % active` selection in AgentUDPSelector with per-packet randomized selection: for each packet, look up `PebbleAgentState[0].Active` to obtain the number of configured workers (`active`), call `bpf_get_prandom_u32()` to get a 32‑bit pseudo-random value, compute `slot = random % active`, and invoke `bpf_sk_select_reuseport(reuse, &pebble_udp_targets, &slot, 0)` exactly once.

Keep using the existing `pebble_agent_state` and `pebble_udp_targets` maps without adding new maps or user-space configuration: `Active` remains the only field, set by Go to the worker count; the BPF program is otherwise stateless and depends only on generic helpers (`bpf_get_prandom_u32`) and the reuseport metadata.

By making the selection independent for each packet and uniformly random across `[0, active)`, packets from a small number of client flows are evenly distributed over all workers over time, ensuring all 6 reuseport sockets share both GET and SCAN load, which reduces per-worker queue depth, mitigates head-of-line blocking for GETs, and allows aggregate throughput to scale closer to the theoretical capacity of all workers.
risks: The design assumes that `bpf_get_prandom_u32()` is available and permitted in sk_reuseport programs on the target kernel; this is expected but not guaranteed solely from the codebase and should be confirmed against the actual runtime environment (uncertain).

Per-packet random selection eliminates flow affinity entirely; while this is safe for the current stateless server and pipelined, reqID-based client, any future features that rely on per-client or per-flow affinity (e.g., per-client rate limiting, stateful sessions) would need to either opt into a different selector policy or reintroduce some form of affinity.

Randomized load balancing provides good balance in expectation but can still produce short-term bursts on individual workers; at very high loads, transient imbalance might slightly increase tail latency relative to an ideal clairvoyant scheduler, though this is likely far smaller than the imbalance caused by the existing flow-hash scheme (uncertain magnitude).

The Go struct `AgentSelectorAgentState` currently contains only an `Active uint32` field; any future changes to the C definition of `struct agent_state` used by `pebble_agent_state` must be accompanied by regenerating the ebpfutil bindings to avoid layout mismatches between BPF and Go.

architecture: Replace the per-flow consistent hashing in agent_udp_selector with a per-packet, time-salted hash that breaks flow stickiness while remaining stateless: on each packet, read `agent_state.active` as the number of available workers, obtain a fast monotonically-increasing timestamp via a BPF helper (e.g., `ktime_get_ns`), combine it with `reuse->hash` using a simple operation (such as XOR), and map the result into `[0, active)` to choose the target slot for a single `bpf_sk_select_reuseport` call.

This design keeps using the existing pebble_agent_state map (no new maps, no extra fields required) but stops relying on `reuse->hash % active`, so packets from a small number of client flows are evenly distributed across all active workers over time, naturally balancing both GET and SCAN load without any explicit per-flow or per-worker state.

Because selection is per-packet and independent of any session state, every worker will see approximately the same share of total traffic (and of the rare long SCANs), which reduces per-worker queuing, mitigates head-of-line blocking for GETs, and allows aggregate throughput to scale up to the true capacity of all 6 workers under the existing synthetic workload.
risks: The design assumes that the server’s request handling is fully stateless per packet and that no Go code maintains per-client or per-flow state that depends on all packets from a given 4‑tuple arriving on the same worker; if such state exists, breaking flow affinity could cause correctness issues.

It is assumed but not yet verified from the code that no other components (e.g., metrics, debugging tools) rely on the current consistent mapping between client flow and worker index for interpretation; changing the selection policy could make some existing logs less intuitive if they implicitly expect per-flow stickiness.

The proposal relies on using a time-based BPF helper (such as `bpf_ktime_get_ns`) from within an sk_reuseport program; while this should be supported on the target kernel, it needs to be confirmed against the actual kernel and BPF helper set used in this environment.

The current Go initialization of the pebble_agent_state map for the 'agent' policy must not depend on any specific struct layout beyond the 'active' field; if it does (e.g., uses padding or assumes a particular size), we need to be careful when regenerating eBPF assets so that any minor changes in the C struct are reflected correctly in the generated Go bindings.

Because the new selector eliminates per-flow affinity, per-flow ordering of packets is no longer guaranteed at the worker level; for this synthetic storage emulator this appears safe, but we should verify that no future extensions or tests assume ordered processing on a per-flow basis.

rag_answers.question: In internal/server/ebpf.go, in the loadEBPF function’s case for the 'agent' policy, how is the PebbleAgentState map initialised exactly (which fields of the generated value struct are written, and with what values)?

answer.answer:
When `loadEBPF` is called with the `"agent"` policy, it calls `loadAgent(workers)`. Inside `loadAgent`, after loading the eBPF objects, it initialises the `PebbleAgentState` map as follows:

1. It declares a key of type `uint32` and sets it to 0:
   - `var key uint32 = 0`

2. It creates a value of type `ebpfutil.AgentSelectorAgentState` and sets only its `Active` field to the provided `workers` count, cast to `uint32`:
   - `state := ebpfutil.AgentSelectorAgentState{ Active: uint32(workers), }`

3. If `objs.PebbleAgentState` is non-nil, it performs an `Update` on the map with that single key–value pair using `ebpf.UpdateAny`:
   - `objs.PebbleAgentState.Update(&key, &state, ebpf.UpdateAny)`

No other fields of the `AgentSelectorAgentState` struct are written; only the `Active` field is set to `uint32(workers)` and stored under key `0`.

rag_answers.question: In the generated bindings under internal/ebpfutil for the agent selector, what is the exact Go struct definition (type name and field list) corresponding to the C struct agent_state used by the pebble_agent_state map?

Under ebpf/ (or wherever the other sk_reuseport selectors live), is there an existing selector program (e.g., for the 'scan_split' or 'hash' policy) that reads from reuse->data / reuse->data_end to inspect the UDP payload, and if so, what does its core bounds-checking pattern for accessing the payload look like?

answer.answer:
The Go server code configures and attaches existing sk_reuseport selector programs for the `scan_split`, `hash`, and `round_robin` policies (`SplitUdpSelector`, `HashUdpSelector`, and `RrUdpSelector` respectively), but the actual eBPF program code that implements those selectors (including any logic that would read from `reuse->data` / `reuse->data_end` and perform bounds checks on the UDP payload) is not present in the provided files. The Go layer only:

1. Loads the compiled eBPF object collections for each policy (`ScanSplitSelectorObjects`, `HashSelectorObjects`, `RrSelectorObjects`).
2. Optionally initializes per-policy state maps (e.g., `PebbleSplitState`, `PebbleHashState`, `PebbleRrState`) with an `Active` worker count (and `Counter` for round robin).
3. Attaches the selected eBPF program to the listening socket via `SO_ATTACH_REUSEPORT_EBPF`.

No UDP payload inspection or `reuse->data` / `reuse->data_end` access patterns are shown in these files, so the core bounds-checking pattern for payload access cannot be determined from the available code.

rag_answers.question: In internal/server/server.go, does handleRequest or any other server code maintain state keyed by the remote UDP address (e.g., maps keyed by net.UDPAddr or IP/port) that would rely on all packets from a given client 4‑tuple consistently arriving on the same worker?

answer.answer:
No. The shown server logic does not maintain any state keyed by the remote UDP address or client 4‑tuple.

The request handler `handleRequest` is fully stateless with respect to client identity: it parses the incoming payload, optionally records timing metrics in a per‑worker `workerStats` entry, and returns a response. It does not access or store any `net.UDPAddr`, IP/port, or similar per‑client key. The only state it touches is:
- The per‑worker stats slice `s.stats[idx]` identified solely by worker index `idx`.
- Configuration fields like delays and maximum scan keys.

The worker‑opening code similarly configures and returns a UDP listener and file descriptor, with no map or other structure keyed by client address. As a result, there is nothing in this code that depends on all packets from a given client arriving on the same worker.

rag_answers.question: In cmd/workload_client/main.go, within the per-worker send goroutine, does the main loop issue multiple outstanding requests on a single UDPConn without waiting for their responses (true pipelining), or does it wait for a response before sending the next request on that socket?

answer.answer: The per-worker send goroutine issues requests continuously on the same UDPConn without ever waiting for a response before sending the next one. The loop only waits on the rate limiter (`limiter.Wait(ctx)`) and then immediately sends another request; it does not perform any read or synchronization with the receive path. Responses are handled by a separate receive goroutine that shares the same `*net.UDPConn`, so multiple outstanding requests are in flight concurrently on each UDPConn (true pipelining).

Reduce GET p99 latency at higher offered loads (≥100k req/s) by shrinking per-worker queues and spreading rare, long SCAN requests across all workers instead of a few hotspots.
Keep the eBPF selector simple, stateless, and O(1) per packet, with no new user-space configuration or additional maps.

Preserve the server’s stateless per-request semantics and the client’s existing pipelined, reqID-based request/response handling so that responses remain correct regardless of which worker processes a given packet.
evidence: The current agent selector computes `start = reuse->hash % state->active` and then probes from that slot, which pins each client 4‑tuple to a fixed worker index, implementing per-flow consistent hashing.

With ~7 client send workers and 6 server workers, server logs show only 4–5 workers handle traffic; each active worker’s GET count per second is an integer multiple of a common base, and those multiples sum to ≈7, confirming that flows are pinned and unevenly packed into 6 buckets.

At offered rates of 50–80k req/s, these 4–5 hot workers still have headroom, so UDP and in-process queues stay short: client sent≈recv, there are no missing responses, and GET p99 latency is only a few microseconds above the synthetic 10µs delay.

At 100k and 140k req/s, total server throughput plateaus around 90–95k req/s even as offered load increases and at least one worker remains idle in each run, indicating that the bottleneck is uneven worker utilization rather than total CPU capacity.

Each worker is a single goroutine that synchronously processes GET (10µs busy-wait) and SCAN (2ms busy-wait) requests in FIFO order; although SCANs are only ~1% of requests, they dominate CPU time (~67%), so when traffic is concentrated on a few workers, those 2ms SCANs repeatedly cause head-of-line blocking for the many short GETs queued behind them.

Under high load, these hot workers’ UDP receive queues and in-process queues grow, pushing GET p99 latency from microseconds to ~0.6ms at 100k and ~5ms at 140k, and eventually overflowing so that ~222k responses are never received at 140k even though the server logs show no application-level errors.

Server-side code (handleRequest and worker setup) is fully stateless with respect to client identity: there is no state keyed by remote UDP address or 4‑tuple, only per-worker stats indexed by worker ID. This means breaking flow affinity does not threaten correctness within the current design.

On the client side, each send goroutine continuously issues requests on its UDPConn under a rate limiter without waiting for responses; a separate recv goroutine on the same UDPConn handles replies and uses embedded reqIDs for matching. Multiple outstanding requests per flow and response reordering are already supported by design, so changing worker selection per packet will not violate any ordering assumptions.
architecture: Replace the flow-sticky `reuse->hash % active` selection in AgentUDPSelector with per-packet randomized selection: for each packet, look up `PebbleAgentState[0].Active` to obtain the number of configured workers (`active`), call `bpf_get_prandom_u32()` to get a 32‑bit pseudo-random value, compute `slot = random % active`, and invoke `bpf_sk_select_reuseport(reuse, &pebble_udp_targets, &slot, 0)` exactly once.

Keep using the existing `pebble_agent_state` and `pebble_udp_targets` maps without adding new maps or user-space configuration: `Active` remains the only field, set by Go to the worker count; the BPF program is otherwise stateless and depends only on generic helpers (`bpf_get_prandom_u32`) and the reuseport metadata.

By making the selection independent for each packet and uniformly random across `[0, active)`, packets from a small number of client flows are evenly distributed over all workers over time, ensuring all 6 reuseport sockets share both GET and SCAN load, which reduces per-worker queue depth, mitigates head-of-line blocking for GETs, and allows aggregate throughput to scale closer to the theoretical capacity of all workers.
risks: The design assumes that `bpf_get_prandom_u32()` is available and permitted in sk_reuseport programs on the target kernel; this is expected but not guaranteed solely from the codebase and should be confirmed against the actual runtime environment (uncertain).

Per-packet random selection eliminates flow affinity entirely; while this is safe for the current stateless server and pipelined, reqID-based client, any future features that rely on per-client or per-flow affinity (e.g., per-client rate limiting, stateful sessions) would need to either opt into a different selector policy or reintroduce some form of affinity.

Randomized load balancing provides good balance in expectation but can still produce short-term bursts on individual workers; at very high loads, transient imbalance might slightly increase tail latency relative to an ideal clairvoyant scheduler, though this is likely far smaller than the imbalance caused by the existing flow-hash scheme (uncertain magnitude).

The Go struct `AgentSelectorAgentState` currently contains only an `Active uint32` field; any future changes to the C definition of `struct agent_state` used by `pebble_agent_state` must be accompanied by regenerating the ebpfutil bindings to avoid layout mismatches between BPF and Go.
